geographic_scope: Statewide (500 ft horizontal / 200 ft vertical buffer around Department of Corrections facilities)
source_title: Operation of Unmanned Aircraft System Over a Department of Corrections Facility Prohibited
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 500 ft horizontal / 200 ft vertical of a Department of Corrections facility; using a UAS to conduct surveillance of, photograph, or record a facility
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — narrow exception categories require prior written Commissioner permission
public_agency_only: No — but several exceptions apply only to government/utility actors
summary: Ala. Code § 13A-7-91 prohibits operating a UAS within 500 ft horizontal or 200 ft vertical of a Department of Corrections 'facility' (defined broadly to include the facility itself, DOC-owned/leased real property out to the outermost physical barrier, and any public road within 100 yards of that barrier, including facilities under construction), or using a UAS to conduct surveillance of, photograph, or record a facility. Exceptions apply to the Department itself, a federally authorized operator flying lawfully, the U.S. Armed Forces, and the Alabama National Guard without further permission; a DOC contractor, a responding law-enforcement/public-safety agency, an emergency-management official, or a state/federal public utility may operate only with the Commissioner's prior written permission. Violation is a Class C felony with a minimum $2,500 fine and a mandatory, non-suspendable 30-day minimum jail/prison sentence.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any project within 500 ft/200 ft of an Alabama Department of Corrections facility as requiring the Commissioner's prior written permission before flying — there is no general commercial-operator or FAA-compliance exemption comparable to some other states' critical-infrastructure carve-outs.
practical_interpretation_agency_practiti: Contact the official or office designated by the cited authority before fixing mobilization dates. Request the current form, documentation checklist, fees, submission route, and processing estimate; retain the issued approval and all site-specific conditions with the flight record.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the Commissioner's written permission (date, scope, facility) in the project file before any correctional-facility-adjacent flight, given the mandatory non-suspendable jail sentence; confirm the facility boundary definition (which extends to a 100-yard public-road buffer) before planning a flight path near any Alabama prison or jail, including one under construction.

source_title: Unauthorized Entry of a Critical Infrastructure Facility (UAS Weapon-Attachment Enhancement)
regulated_activity: Unauthorized entry (including via UAS) of an enclosed/posted critical infrastructure facility; separately, possessing or operating a UAS with an attached weapon, firearm, explosive, destructive device, or ammunition while committing unauthorized entry of such a facility
requirement_type: Prohibition (misdemeanor; felony for weapon-attached UAS or for interrupting/damaging facility operations)
summary: Ala. Code § 13A-7-4.3 defines 'critical infrastructure facility' extensively (chemical/refinery/pipeline facilities, electrical generation/transmission/distribution infrastructure, water/wastewater systems, natural gas and LNG facilities, mining operations, transportation facilities including ports/airports/railroads, communications infrastructure, dams, defense contractor facilities, steelmaking facilities using electric-arc furnaces, and pulp/paper manufacturing facilities, among others). Unauthorized entry of such a facility that is enclosed by a physical barrier or conspicuously posted is a Class A misdemeanor; intentionally, recklessly, or negligently damaging critical infrastructure property or interrupting its operations is a Class C felony. A person who commits unauthorized entry of such a facility while possessing or operating a UAS with an attached weapon, firearm, explosive, destructive device, or ammunition is guilty of a Class C felony (subsection (e)) — this UAS-specific enhancement applies to weapon-attached UAS entry, not to ordinary UAS overflight or photography alone. An exception preserves lawful assembly/petition activity, including labor disputes, and an employment-scope exception applies to work necessary for a lawful work assignment.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: The UAS-specific felony enhancement in this statute is narrow — it targets weapon-attached UAS combined with unauthorized physical entry, not ordinary aerial photography or inspection overflight of critical infrastructure. Standard AEC infrastructure-inspection UAS work (no attached weapon, no unauthorized physical entry) is not the conduct this enhancement targets, but confirm site access authorization before any flight involving physical entry to an enclosed or posted facility.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Distinguish this statute's narrow UAS-weapon enhancement from a general UAS-overflight prohibition — it does not on its face prohibit routine aerial photography of critical infrastructure from outside the facility's enclosed/posted boundary. Document facility access authorization for any work requiring physical entry.

source_title: Counter-UAS Mitigation Authority for Department of Corrections Facilities
citation: Ala. Code § 13A-7-94.1 (added by HB 274, 2026 Regular Session)
regulated_party: Alabama Department of Corrections (not a private-operator restriction)
regulated_activity: Detecting, tracking, and mitigating (including jamming, hacking, or physical capture) a UAS operating in violation of § 13A-7-91 near a DOC facility
requirement_type: Agency enforcement authority (not a permit requirement for private operators)
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for private operators; High for situational awareness near DOC facilities
summary: HB 274 (2026 Regular Session), effective June 1, 2026, adds § 13A-7-94.1 to authorize the Alabama Department of Corrections to take reasonable and necessary measures to mitigate a UAS operating in violation of § 13A-7-91 (AL-001) near a DOC facility, including signal jamming (to the extent consistent with federal law and FCC regulations), hacking, physical capture, or other reasonable mitigation to neutralize, intercept, disable, or disrupt the UAS. This is an agency enforcement-authority statute, not an additional restriction on private operators beyond § 13A-7-91 itself.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This does not create a new prohibition for AEC operators beyond § 13A-7-91 (AL-001), but it materially raises the practical risk of an authorized correctional-facility UAS flight being electronically interfered with or physically disabled if it strays into the restricted zone without prior written Commissioner permission — budget extra margin around the 500 ft/200 ft buffer.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: This is not a categorical purchasing ban, but it creates potential equipment-loss exposure near protected locations. Consider loss risk, insurance treatment, geofencing configuration, and replaceability when assigning aircraft to work in the affected environment.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: No new private-operator compliance obligation is created by this statute itself; it is relevant context when advising a client on the practical enforcement risk (equipment loss/damage from lawful state countermeasures) of flying near an Alabama correctional facility without documented permission under § 13A-7-91.
verification_status: Enactment, effective date, and substance corroborated by contemporaneous Alabama news coverage (mynbc15.com, wsfa.com) reporting the bill's passage and June 1, 2026 effective date; the enrolled bill PDF was located but its full text was not independently read in this pass.
notes: Recommend direct verification of the enrolled HB 274 text against the codified § 13A-7-94.1 once fully incorporated into the official Code of Alabama.

regulated_activity: Hunting, taking, capturing, or killing (or attempting to) any bird or animal with the aid of an aircraft (among other listed mechanized devices)
summary: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.11(1)(a) makes it unlawful to concentrate, drive, rally, molest, hunt, take, capture, or kill (or attempt to) any bird or animal with the aid of an automobile, aircraft, train, motorboat, sailboat, or other mechanically propelled device or device operated in conjunction with one. The rule's text uses the general term 'aircraft' and does not separately define or specifically name unmanned aircraft, UAS, or drones; this record is included because 'aircraft' is a plausible plain-language match for a drone, but no Alabama Game and Fish Division guidance expressly confirming that this rule applies to UAS was located during this research pass.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat this rule as likely — but not conclusively confirmed — to prohibit using a drone to locate, drive, or aid in taking wildlife, and apply the same conservative standoff practice used in states with an express UAS-hunting prohibition until Game and Fish Division guidance confirms the rule's scope.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Flag the interpretive gap for the client: the rule's 'aircraft' language has not been confirmed by agency guidance or case law to include unmanned aircraft; a direct inquiry to the Alabama Department of Conservation and Natural Resources is recommended before relying on this rule's silence as evidence that UAS use is unregulated for hunting-adjacent purposes.

summary: Alabama has not enacted a comprehensive statewide UAS-preemption statute comparable to Georgia's or Arizona's. Secondary sources describe Alabama as recognizing the FAA as the sole regulator of navigable airspace and preempting local governments from establishing airspace no-fly zones without FAA approval, but otherwise leaving room for a municipal ordinance patchwork — for example, the City of Oxford's Ordinance 2016-28 (barring drone flights over city-owned property, reportedly used as a template by other Alabama cities) and Orange Beach's ordinance restricting UAS operation within 500 ft of a venue, outdoor special event, or Gulf beach area absent FAA and city-administrator permission.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not assume Alabama state law displaces local drone ordinances — confirm municipal rules for any project site, particularly in coastal/tourism municipalities (e.g., Orange Beach) and any city that has adopted an Oxford-style city-property ban, in a later research phase before finalizing site-specific flight plans.

practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Flag for the client that Alabama's local-ordinance landscape is largely unconstrained by state preemption; advise a jurisdiction-specific ordinance check before relying on this state-level summary alone for a specific Alabama project site.
